pairs.es: Which point on the diagram represents the earthquake epicenter?
pairs.en: Point D — the single point where the distance circles from all three seismograph stations (A, B, C) intersect.

pairs.es: What is the name of the method shown for locating an earthquake epicenter?
pairs.en: Triangulation — using the P-wave and S-wave arrival time difference from at least three seismograph stations to find the epicenter.

pairs.es: Why do the 'Shadow zone — No waves received' areas exist?
pairs.en: The liquid outer core blocks S-waves entirely and refracts P-waves away, creating zones on the opposite side of Earth where no seismic waves arrive.

pairs.es: At point B (bottom of the diagram), only one type of wave is received. Which type, and why?
pairs.en: Only P-waves. S-waves cannot travel through Earth's liquid outer core, so they never reach point B. P-waves can pass through liquids and still arrive.

pairs.es: Which labeled point(s) (A, B, C, or D) are located in the shadow zone?
pairs.en: Points B and C — they are positioned on the far side of Earth in the region where seismic waves are deflected by the liquid outer core.

pairs.es: What does the star (✶) represent in Diagram 1?
pairs.en: The earthquake epicenter — the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus (underground origin point of the earthquake).

pairs.es: Which station (I, II, III, or IV) is closest to the earthquake epicenter, and how can you tell?
pairs.en: Station I — P-waves and S-waves arrive very close together, meaning a small time gap and shorter distance to the epicenter.

pairs.es: Station IV shows only P-wave arrival with no S-wave. What does this indicate?
pairs.en: Station IV is in the shadow zone. S-waves cannot pass through Earth's liquid outer core, so they never reach Station IV.

pairs.es: What does a larger time gap between P-wave arrival and S-wave arrival indicate?
pairs.en: The seismograph station is farther from the earthquake epicenter. Stations I → II → III show increasing P-S gaps = increasing distance.
